landmarks.name: Avenue of the Baobabs
landmarks.writeup: A famous dirt road lined with towering baobab trees, iconic for its unique landscape and sunset views.

wiki.extract: The Avenue of the Baobabs, or Alley of the Baobabs, is a prominent group of Grandidier's baobabs lining the unpaved Road No.8 between Morondava and Belon'i Tsiribihina in the Menabe region of western Madagascar. Its striking landscape draws travelers from around the world, making it one of the most visited locations in the region. It has been a center of local conservation efforts, and was granted temporary protected status in July 2007 by the Ministry of Environment, Water and Forestry – a step toward making it Madagascar's first natural monument.

landmarks.name: Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park
landmarks.writeup: A UNESCO World Heritage site known for its limestone karst formations and rich biodiversity.

wiki.extract: The Tsingy de Bemaraha National Park is a national park located in northwest Madagascar. It is mainly within the boundaries of Antsalova District, with a small part in the northeast falling within Morafenobe District. The national park centers on two geological formations: the Great Tsingy and the Little Tsingy. Together with the adjacent Tsingy de Bemaraha Strict Nature Reserve, the National Park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

landmarks.name: Ranomafana National Park
landmarks.writeup: A rainforest park home to rare lemurs and diverse flora and fauna.

wiki.extract: Ranomafana National Park is a national park in southeastern Madagascar, in the Haute Matsiatra and Vatovavy regions. It was established as Madagascar's fourth national park in 1991 following the rediscovery of the greater bamboo lemur and the discovery of the golden bamboo lemur by the primatologist Dr. Patricia Wright.

cultural_events.name: Famadihana (Turning of the Bones)
cultural_events.writeup: A traditional Malagasy funerary custom where families exhume ancestors' remains, rewrap them, and celebrate their memory.

wiki.extract: Famadihana is a funerary tradition of the Malagasy peoples of Madagascar. During this ceremony, known as the turning of the bones, people bring forth the bodies of their ancestors from the family crypts, rewrap the corpses in fresh cloth, and rewrite their names on the cloth so they will always be remembered. Then they dance to live music while carrying the corpses over their heads and go around the tomb before returning the corpses to the family tomb. They believe in celebrating the life lived by the dead person.

cultural_events.name: Donia Festival
cultural_events.writeup: An annual music and cultural festival held on Nosy Be island showcasing Malagasy and regional music.

food_writeup: Madagascar's cuisine blends African, Asian, and French influences, featuring rice as a staple, accompanied by dishes with zebu meat, seafood, and diverse spices.
brief_history: Madagascar was first settled by Austronesian peoples around 500 AD, later influenced by African, Arab, and European traders. It became a French colony in 1896 and gained independence in 1960.
current_conflicts: Madagascar faces political instability and social unrest related to governance and economic challenges, but no active armed conflicts.

commentary.inflation_management: Madagascar's inflation has been persistently elevated but never explosive, averaging around 7-9% for much of the period. It peaked at 10.8% in 2006 and troughed at 4.2% in 2020, the series low, when COVID suppressed demand. The ariary floats with management, and the central bank has no formal inflation target, but it has generally kept policy tight enough to avoid spirals. Food prices dominate the index, so cyclones and droughts drive the spikes: 9.9% in 2023 reflected poor harvests. The IMF projects 8.0% for 2025. Monetary policy is credible within its limits, but in Madagascar inflation is mostly a climate story.
commentary.debt_management: Madagascar's debt has been moderate throughout, reflecting limited market access as much as prudence. From 28.2% of GDP in 2007, the series low, it drifted upward as governments borrowed concessionally for infrastructure: 52.9% in 2020, the series high, after COVID spending, easing to a projected 49.2% in 2025. The debt is overwhelmingly concessional (World Bank, AfDB), which keeps servicing manageable, and IMF assessments judge the risk of distress moderate. The constraint is not the level but the use: borrowing has not translated into transformative infrastructure, and climate shocks repeatedly destroy what is built.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued moderate growth with inflation near 7-8% and debt around 50% of GDP, all hostage to climate. Upside comes from mining (nickel, cobalt) and tourism; downside is the next cyclone or drought, which regularly wipes out a year's gains. Uncertainty is moderate: the macro framework is stable, but Madagascar's economy is among the world's most climate-vulnerable, and that dominates the outlook.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
